experiments.Conclusion: The City earns more because of evening trade and a larger market.
experiments.Question: Which location earns most?
experiments.Strategic reading: Same strategy, different market: the City's evening trade and larger market raised the ceiling.

experiments.What changed: Campus at parity vs City at a premium
experiments.Conclusion: Low rent and 5-star customers cannot offset a small, price-sensitive market.
experiments.Question: Can the cheapest site win on low price?
experiments.Strategic reading: Cost leadership failed where $1 vending machines and price-sensitive students capped the price. A Five Forces problem, not an execution problem.

experiments.Conclusion: Location sets the ceiling; strategy decides how close you get.
experiments.Question: City or Suburb with the same best strategy?
experiments.Strategic reading: Even with the best strategy, location sets the ceiling; strategy decides how close you get to it.

experiments.Conclusion: A $1,000 lead keeps staff at 5 stars.
experiments.Question: Is a $2,000 pay lead needed?
experiments.Strategic reading: A modest pay lead was enough to keep 5-star staff. Beyond that, wages were cost without extra sales.

experiments.Conclusion: No: sales fall by more than the saving.
experiments.Question: Can training be cut to $1,000?
experiments.Strategic reading: Training is not a cost to trim: cutting it lost 11 drinks a day, worth more than the saving.

experiments.Conclusion: No: sales unchanged, so the extra spend is wasted.
experiments.Question: Does promotion above $10,000 help?
experiments.Strategic reading: Promotion has a saturation point. Above $10,000 it bought no extra customers.

experiments.Conclusion: Yes, through 7–8% more customers, not through cost savings.
experiments.Question: Does roasting our own beans pay?
experiments.Strategic reading: Roasting paid through differentiation, not cost: the cup saving alone would have lost about $60,000. Extra customers made the difference.

experiments.Conclusion: Yes: about twice their cost, and customers reach 5 stars at a premium.
experiments.Question: Do organic beans pay?
experiments.Strategic reading: Sustainability paid: organic beans returned about twice their cost and won 5-star ratings at a premium price.

experiments.What changed: One extra employee kept for 5 years
experiments.Conclusion: No: demand rises only in the hiring year. A people-versus-profit trade-off.
experiments.Question: Does one extra job pay for itself?
experiments.Strategic reading: The people goal had a price. The game rewarded hiring only in the year it happened.

experiments.Conclusion: Larger lift in the Suburb; about $24,000 of the gain is pay and training tuning.
experiments.Question: Roast + organic in the Suburb?
experiments.Strategic reading: Quality investments paid even more where customers value locally roasted coffee. About $24,000 of this gain came from pay and training tuning.

experiments.What changed: Roasting in Mature: yes vs no
experiments.Conclusion: Yes: about 20 more drinks per store per day, every year.
experiments.Question: Is roasting worth it in Mature markets?
experiments.Strategic reading: Vertical integration pays where customers value the result: Mature customers bought about 20 more drinks per store per day.

experiments.What changed: Roasting in Emerging: yes vs no
experiments.Conclusion: No: the small lift does not cover roaster depreciation.
experiments.Question: Is roasting worth it in Emerging markets?
experiments.Strategic reading: In Emerging Markets the lift was too small to cover a roaster's $20,000 a year, although the gap narrowed as prices rose.

experiments.What changed: 3 more Emerging own stores a year, Years 2–4
experiments.Conclusion: Yes: profit dips for two years, then overtakes.
experiments.Question: Open Emerging own stores faster?
experiments.Strategic reading: Judge growth on future store economics, not this year's profit: Run 2 trailed for two years, then overtook by $953K.

experiments.What changed: 3 Emerging own stores in Year 1, not 2
experiments.Conclusion: Yes: level by Year 3, ahead afterwards; no loss of sales per store.
experiments.Question: Open one more Emerging store in Year 1?
experiments.Strategic reading: Open early while each new store can still repay its $100,000 opening cost: level by Year 3, ahead afterwards.

rules.Question: Choosing a site or market
rules.What changed: Pick the largest market with evening demand
rules.Conclusion: Low rent cannot fix a small market

rules.Question: Recession
rules.Runs compared: Recession: matching rivals lifted drinks 6.5% (Levels 1 and 3)
rules.Conclusion: A discount below rivals was never tested

rules.Question: Good economy or recovery
rules.Runs compared: Recovery: 14–20% price rises cost only 4.7–5.9% of volume
rules.Conclusion: Customers drop to 4 stars without brand support (roasting, organic)

rules.Question: Staff
rules.Conclusion: Higher training was not tested cleanly

rules.Question: Roasting and premium beans
rules.What changed: Invest only where customers value them
rules.Conclusion: The Emerging penalty shrank as prices rose

rules.Question: Franchising
rules.Runs compared: Franchises earned $6.45M before shared costs (Level 3 Run 5)
rules.Conclusion: Relies on keeping customers at 5 stars

rules.Question: Own stores
rules.What changed: Open early and at the maximum; stop in the final year
rules.Conclusion: Expect a profit dip first; yearly feedback will look bad
